2. The facts relevant for the disposal of this Rule are as follows:—The petitioner claiming to be a co-sharer by purchase filed an application on 19.12.77 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-empting the land measuring 91. Acre purchased by opposite-parties Nos. 1 to 3 by a document executed on 26.1.74 and registered on 23.8.74. The petitioner also stated that he has about 3/4 bighas of land. 

 5. The vendees, opposite-party Nos. 1 to 3, preferred an appeal, being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 27 of 1980. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal by the impugned judgment and order dated 27.4.81. The appellate Court noticed that the appellants took the plea in the pre-empt ion case that there was an agreement for reconveyance with the vendors, but observed that "it appears that the land was returned to the vendors after the filing of the case on 19.12.77." On the point of Section 90 of S.A. & T. Act, the appellate Court observed that in paragraph 2 of the petition they (pre-emptor is one only) stated that they have land not more than 3/4 bighas, but there is no evidence to that effect. Then, relying on a decision, reported in 29. D.L.R. 153, the appellate Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the pre-emption case for want of evidence and finding of the court as to the bar of section 90 of the S.A. & T. Act. 

 "There is no dispute that a person seeking pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act must show that he is a person entitled to purchase or acquire land within the maximum ceiling as set out in section 90. But mere omission to make an assertion in his application or to adduce evidence to this effect, in the absence of any averment to the contrary, will not render the application liable to be dismissed. 

 7. In the instant case there is a statement in paragraph 2 of the petition to the effect that the petitioner has got 3/4 bighas of land, which has also been noticed by the appellate Court, and there is no denial of this assertion in the written objection filed by the vendee opposite-parties. The learned Munsif found that there is no other bar of section 90 standing in the way of the petitioner to pre-empt." yet the appellate court observed that nowhere in the judgment there is compliance of section 90 of S.A. & T Act. Therefore, in the light of the decisions of the Appellate Division and the Division Bench of the High Court Division referred to above, the judgment of the appellate Court below dismissing the pre-emption case cannot be sustained, but that, however, does not conclude the matter. The vendee-opposite parties in their written objection have stated that they have already returned the land with possession to the opposite-party Nos. 4-6(Vendors) by a registered deed on 11.3.78 on receiving back the consideration money from them, in pursuance of on oral agreement to that effect, and that they have filed the certified copy of the said deed therewith. The said document of reconveyance was filed but has not been proved in the case. The trial court disbelieved the story of oral agreement and found the reconveyance after the institution of thy pre-emption case to be collusive and fraudulent. The appellate Court while reversing the trial court's judgment simply noticed that "the land was returned to the vendors after filing of the case on 19.12.77." The pre-emption case was filed on 19.12.77, and reconveyance of the land under pre-emption took place on 11.3.78; and the judgment of the trial court was passed on 30.1.80 allowing pre-emption. Therefore, the legal consequence of such a reconveyance of the land under pre-emption to the vendors during the pendency of the pre-emption proceedings is to be considered in order to determine if the sale in that case remains subsisting to sustain the pre-emption case. Since the story of oral agreement for reconveyance has been disbelieved it is to be taken as retransfer to the vendors without any agreement for reconveyance. In the event of reconveyance of the land under pre-emption the vendor before the commencement of pre-emption proceeding the sale in favour of the vendee does not remain subsisting, and the right of pre-emption also ceases to exist, and so, pre-emption case cannot be instituted on the basis thereof. This is the view taken in two decisions of a Single Bench of the Dhaka High Court, reported in 29 DLR 229 and 1 B.C.R.(1981) at page 27. The matter has been finally settled by the Appellate Division in the case of Shafi Khan Vs. Mannujan Hussain and others, reported in 35 D.L.R. (AD) 225. Their Lordships concluded the matter in paragraph 7 in the following terms: "The question before us is simple, whether the sale by Abdul Bari Khan which took place on 28th March, 1974 remained in force when the petition for pre-emption was filed on 1.11.74. The obvious answer is that there was no transfer subsisting on 1.11.74 simply because the land went back to the vendor on 31.10.74. The right to pre-emption is therefore, not available as the original vendor and co-sharer got back already his ownership in its entirety, it being immaterial whether he got back his ownership in pursuance of an agreement for reconveyance or independent of any such agreement. The main question for careful examination will be whether he actually got back his land, and if the answer is in the affirmative, the positions will he as if no transfer was at all made by him." If I have understood the decision of the Appellate Division aright. its means that in the event of re-transfer of the land in question by the vendee in favour of the vendor by a valid deed, as distinguished from a subsequent transfer by the vendee to a third party, before the commencement of pre-emption proceeding, the sale is completely wiped out it is rendered non est. and the right to pre-emption arising from the original sale is nipped in the bud, and no cause or action survives for initiating a proceeding for pre-eruption. 

 10. Before attempting to give a satisfactory answer to the question raised in the case, it will be convenient to notice the material incidents of the right of pre-emption in terms of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, hereinafter referred to as the Act, While considering an appeal arising from a pre-emption case under Punjab Pre-emption Act (Act 1 of 1913) the Indian Supreme Court made certain general observations regarding the character of the right of pre-emotion, which may be of some help in understanding the nature of the right of pre-emption as provided in section 96 of the Act. The decision is in the case of Bishan Singh and others Vs. Khazau Singh and another, reported in A.I.R. 1958, (S.C.) at page 838. In paragraph 7 of the said report their Lord-ships quoted a passage from a decision of Plowden, 3. which is as follows: 

 Now coming to the provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it appears to me that the section is founded on the recognition of pre-emptor's primary right to the offer of the property about to be sold, and provides both the machinery and the method for enforcing the Secondary right of pursuing the property sold in disregard of his preference, if the preemptor thinks fit. It confers a right to purchase a holding or a share or portion thereof sold through the coercive process of the court. It does not create in favour of the pre-emptor a right to or in the property sold till the final order is made under section 96(7) of the Act. Before the final order is made accepting the preference of the pre-emptor it is a mere claim to purchase, which may or may not be sustained in the end. In terms of the section the transfer by the vendor gives rise to a right of coercive transfer through court in favour of the pre-emptor. It is a right to be substituted in the place of the vendee, if, the pre-emptor can establish his right superior to that of the vendee. If the final order cannot be made under sub-section (7) of section 96 of the Act for any reason, the pre-emptor does not acquire any interest in the property sold. The section takes for granted that the right of the pre-emptor to pre-empt and the sale giving rise to cause of action will subsist till the final order is made. If the pre-emptor's interest in the holding is lost or the sale is rendered non-existent the proceeding for pre-emption becomes infructuous. The object of the section is to direct transfer of the land under pre-emption from the pre-emptee to the preemptor on the basis of latter's preference in the matter. The section is designed to achieve the priority in the matter of transfer of property as envisaged in sub-section (5) thereof. The primary right to the offer of the property about to be sold having been dis-regarded by the vendor, the section ensures the pre-emptor of enforcing the priority in the matter of transfer of such property, if he so desires to pursue it. 

 In that case the transferor instituted a suit impeaching the transferee under pre-emption (heba) during the pendency of the pre-emption case, and obtained an exparte decree, and on that basis the transferee resisted the pre-emption petition under section 24 of East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, stating that there was no transfer of the suit land, and so the application for pre-emption was not maintainable. The learned Munsif turned down the objection on the finding that the suit for setting the said transfer by heba was collusive, and allowed pre-emption. The appellate court did not find any collusion in the suit, and so allowed the appeal and dismissed the application for pre-emption. The appellate Court's order disallowing pre-emption was maintained by the High Court, and nothing wrong was found in obtaining the exparte decree setting aside the transfer in question during the pendency of the pre-emption proceeding. A passage from this decision was approvingly quoted by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 225. 

 17. It is well settled that the effect of section 52 of Transfer of Property Act is not to wipe out a sale pendente lite altogether but to subordinate it to the rights based on the decree or the order passed in the proceeding. The transferee pendente lite takes the property subject to the result of the suit or proceeding. It is to be noticed that the right under the decree or order is sought to be protected by the doctrine of lis pendens. But if the proceeding cannot yield any result creating any right in favour of a party to the proceeding, the question of applying the doctrine does not arise. In case of pre-emption proceeding, if the transfer is rendered non est by reconveyance of the property to the vendor; pen dente lite, no final order can be made creating a right in the property in favour of the pre-emptor, and it has already been noticed earlier that such reconveyance by the vendee to the vendor is not prohibited by section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The decisive date is the date of the order passed in the proceeding in terms of the provisions of both section 96 of the Act and section 52 of Transfer of Property Act. So, it appears to me that section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act does not contemplate a re-conveyance of the property to the vendor, thus undoing the transfer under pre-emption and rendering the proceeding based thereon ineffectual.
